Class 8 · Module 3

The Micronutrient Signals: Vitamin D and B12

Two markers that reward a smarter read than "low, normal, or high."

60 min read 9 cited sources

Two people, same lab, same number: 28 ng/mL of vitamin D. The first drew blood in late August after a summer of hiking. The second drew blood in late February after a dark, indoor winter. On paper they are identical. In reality they are on opposite trajectories — one sliding down from a summer peak, the other clawing up from a winter trough. Read as a single snapshot, the number tells you almost nothing about where either person actually lives across the year.

This chapter is about two nutrient markers that dominate self-directed testing and that both punish the snapshot habit. Vitamin D moves predictably with the seasons and with your body. B12 does something sneakier: it can read comfortably "normal" while your cells are quietly starved. Both markers teach the same lesson you met with ferritin last chapter — a single value can look fine and still mislead — but each teaches it in its own way.

Start here: what to actually do

Before the biology, the decisions. If you take nothing else from this chapter, take these.

For vitamin D: Note when the blood was drawn before you interpret the number. A late-winter value and a late-summer value from the same person can differ by roughly 10 ng/mL for no reason other than the calendar (Shoben et al., 2011). Aim to be above the sufficiency line year-round, not just at your August peak — which means your summer number needs headroom. Supplementation moves the marker in a predictable, dose-dependent, and distinctly unmagical way.

For B12: A "normal" serum B12 is reassuring only in the absence of symptoms. If there are neurological complaints — tingling, numbness, balance problems, brain fog — a normal B12 does not close the question. Confirmatory markers exist precisely because the standard test misses functional deficiency (Stabler, 2013). And when a CBC shows enlarged red cells (high MCV), B12 and folate are two of the first suspects.

Everything below explains why these frames work, and how to apply them without overreaching into diagnosis — which remains a clinician's job.

Think About It

Two friends both get vitamin D results of 30 ng/mL. One tested in January, one in July. Without any other information, which one would you be more concerned about heading into the coming months — and why?

Vitamin D is a hormone wearing a nutrient's clothes

We file vitamin D under "vitamins," but biologically it behaves like a prohormone. Your skin makes it from sunlight; your liver and kidneys activate it in two steps; and the active form regulates gene expression in tissues throughout the body (Holick, 2007). That origin story matters for how you read the lab, because a nutrient you eat and a hormone your skin manufactures on demand follow completely different rules.

The standard test measures 25-hydroxyvitamin D, usually written 25(OH)D. This is the storage-and-transport form — the best single indicator of your overall vitamin D status because it reflects everything: what your skin made, what you ate, what you supplemented. It is not the active hormone (that's 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, which is tightly regulated and a poor status marker). When a report says "Vitamin D," it almost always means 25(OH)D. Confirm that before comparing numbers across labs.

A units warning that trips up everyone

Vitamin D is reported in two units, and they are not interchangeable. In the United States you'll usually see ng/mL; much of the rest of the world uses nmol/L. The conversion is:

1 ng/mL ≈ 2.5 nmol/L

So 30 ng/mL equals 75 nmol/L, and 50 nmol/L equals 20 ng/mL. The research literature mixes both freely — several studies cited in this chapter report nmol/L. If a threshold ever looks wildly off, check the units before you check your understanding.

Why the same person drifts across the range all year

Here is the single most under-appreciated fact about vitamin D testing: it is seasonal. In a study of 2,298 older adults, 25(OH)D followed a smooth, wave-like annual pattern with an average peak-to-trough swing of 9.6 ng/mL (Shoben et al., 2011). Levels crest in late summer, several weeks after peak sun, and bottom out in late winter. The lag exists because your body draws down stored vitamin D through the dark months.

That swing is not a rounding error. It is large enough to move you across a decision line. In a sample of nearly 22,000 adults, 63% were predicted to fall below the 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL) insufficiency threshold in late winter — even when their summertime values looked perfectly adequate (Bolland et al., 2008). In other words, a July test can declare you "sufficient" while your February self is quietly deficient. The authors' conclusion is the practical one: the summertime level you need to guarantee year-round sufficiency is higher than the cutoff itself, and it varies by sex, age, and ethnicity.

This is exactly the "read the position in context" theme from earlier in the course, dressed in new clothes. With ferritin, the context was inflammation. With vitamin D, the context is the calendar. Same discipline: never read the dot without asking what's pushing it.

The levers that set your personal curve

Season sets the shape of the wave. Several personal factors set its height:

Latitude. The farther you live from the equator, the weaker the winter sun's UVB — and above roughly 35° latitude, winter sunlight is often too oblique to trigger meaningful skin synthesis at all (Holick, 2007). Higher latitude also produces bigger seasonal swings (Shoben et al., 2011).

Skin pigmentation. Melanin is a natural sunscreen. Darker skin needs substantially more sun exposure to make the same vitamin D, which is a major reason people with darker skin at high latitudes carry higher deficiency risk (Piccolo et al., 2019; Holick, 2007).

Body composition. Vitamin D is fat-soluble, and adipose tissue sequesters it. In overweight and obese adults, sun exposure, skin reflectance, and adiposity together explained the bulk of 25(OH)D variation — with higher body fat pulling serum levels down (Piccolo et al., 2019). People with more body fat often need a higher intake to reach the same serum number.

Time outdoors — and behavior. Sunscreen, clothing, and indoor lifestyles all suppress synthesis. Interestingly, more physically active people showed larger seasonal swings, likely because they get more summer sun (Shoben et al., 2011).

Think About It

Two people live in the same city at the same latitude. One has darker skin and a desk job; the other has lighter skin and gardens daily. Whose vitamin D curve would you expect to sit lower, and which of the four levers above are doing the work?

Sufficient versus optimal: an honest look at a real debate

Here the course's central distinction — "in range" is not the same as "optimal" — sits at the heart of an active scientific disagreement. Not a fringe one. A genuine, unresolved debate among serious researchers.

Most laboratories draw the sufficiency line at 20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L), the level associated with skeletal health for most of the population — the number the Institute of Medicine anchored to bone outcomes. Below about 12 ng/mL is frank deficiency. So far, so standard.

But a body of work argues that the level associated with lowest risk for non-skeletal outcomes — cardiovascular disease, several cancers, diabetes, all-cause mortality — sits meaningfully higher, generally above 30 ng/mL and for some outcomes in the 40–50 ng/mL range (Grant et al., 2022). On this view, "sufficient for bones" and "optimal across the body" are different questions with different answers, and the standard cutoff answers only the first.

Why isn't this settled? Partly because vitamin D trials have a design flaw that Grant and colleagues emphasize: many enrolled people who were already replete, or gave a fixed dose without measuring the achieved blood level. If you give vitamin D to someone who doesn't need it, you shouldn't expect benefit — yet those null results get read as "vitamin D doesn't work." The argument is that trials should target an achieved 25(OH)D concentration, not a dose. Until more trials do, the optimal range remains contested rather than proven.

How to hold a contested target responsibly

You don't have to resolve the debate to act sensibly. A defensible reading:

Below the sufficiency line is a clear sign warranting attention — and if it's paired with symptoms (bone pain, muscle weakness, fatigue), a sign warranting medical evaluation rather than DIY dosing. The gap between ~20 and ~40 ng/mL is where the "sufficient vs. optimal" conversation lives; many practitioners aim toward the upper end of that band, understanding it as reasoned preference informed by observational data, not settled fact. And more is not endlessly better: pushing well above 50–60 ng/mL adds cost and, at high enough sustained levels, risk of toxicity, without established benefit. The honest posture is a target zone held with appropriate humility, not a magic number defended like dogma.

The optimal serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration for many health outcomes appears to be above the level currently defined as sufficient.

Paraphrasing Grant et al. (2022)

How supplementation actually moves the number

People expect vitamin D supplementation to work like flipping a switch. It's more like filling a tank with a hose whose flow slows as the tank fills. The pooled European trial data give us usable numbers: supplementation raised 25(OH)D by an average of 36 nmol/L versus placebo, at roughly 1.77 nmol/L per 2.5 µg (100 IU) per day (Zittermann et al., 2023).

Translate that into a rule of thumb: about 1 ng/mL rise per 100 IU daily, very roughly, for a typical adult. So 1,000 IU/day nudges most people up by around 10 ng/mL over a couple of months. That same analysis found ~1,000 IU daily would lift 95% of healthy European adults above 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL) — enough to clear the sufficiency line, but not necessarily to reach the higher "optimal" targets some pursue.

Two crucial caveats that keep expectations honest:

The response shrinks as you climb. Each additional increment does less than the last — the increase per unit dose decreases at higher doses and higher baseline levels (Zittermann et al., 2023). Going from deficient to sufficient is efficient; squeezing out the last few points toward a high target takes disproportionately more.

Bodies differ. Someone with higher body fat, darker skin, or malabsorption will move less per dose than the average (Piccolo et al., 2019). The rule of thumb is a starting estimate, not a guarantee — which is exactly why you re-test rather than assume.

Think About It

Someone at 22 ng/mL wants to reach a personal target of about 40 ng/mL. Using the rough "1 ng/mL per 100 IU" heuristic, what daily dose gets them into that neighborhood — and why should they re-test rather than trust the arithmetic alone?

B12: the marker that lies with a straight face

If vitamin D's problem is that it moves predictably, B12's problem is worse: the standard test can read normal while the deficiency is real. This is the ferritin trap all over again — a number that looks fine but doesn't tell the whole story — and drawing that parallel is the whole point. Once you've seen two very different markers fail the same way, you stop trusting any single value on faith.

First, a quick refresher. Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is essential for two jobs: making healthy DNA (needed for producing red blood cells) and maintaining the myelin sheath that insulates nerves. When B12 runs short, both systems suffer — you get anemia and you get neurological damage. Crucially, these two consequences don't always arrive together or in order.

The evidence that "normal" isn't enough

The landmark study here is decades old and still bracing. Among 141 patients with neuropsychiatric problems caused by cobalamin deficiency, 28% had no anemia and a normal MCV — their blood counts looked entirely unremarkable (Lindenbaum et al., 1988). Their symptoms were neurological: paresthesias (pins and needles), sensory loss, unsteady gait, cognitive changes. If you had relied on the CBC, you'd have missed more than a quarter of these patients. What confirmed the diagnosis was not serum B12 alone but two downstream markers — methylmalonic acid and homocysteine.

The problem is structural, not occasional. As the clinical literature bluntly states, current serum B12 assays have insufficient sensitivity and specificity — meaning the test both misses true deficiency and flags false ones (Stabler, 2013). Depending on how you define it, subclinical B12 deficiency — low function despite unremarkable standard tests — may affect anywhere from 2.5% to 26% of the general population (Green et al., 2017). That's an enormous range, and it exists precisely because the definition depends on which marker you trust.

The confirmation layers: what B12 is actually doing

Why does serum B12 mislead? Because it measures how much B12 is circulating, not how much is reaching and working inside your cells. Two problems: much of the B12 in your blood is bound to a protein that can't deliver it to tissues, and the number can look fine while cellular supply is inadequate. So we use functional markers — substances that pile up when B12 isn't doing its job.

Methylmalonic acid (MMA). B12 is required to process MMA. When B12 is functionally low, MMA accumulates. Elevated MMA is the most specific confirmatory signal — it's the key test that pins down real deficiency when serum B12 is equivocal (Stabler, 2013; Green et al., 2017).

Homocysteine. Both B12 and folate are needed to clear homocysteine. When either runs low, homocysteine rises. It's sensitive but less specific — it goes up in B12 deficiency and folate deficiency, so it can't distinguish the two on its own.

Holotranscobalamin ("active B12"). This measures only the fraction of B12 actually available to cells, offering an earlier read than total serum B12 (Green et al., 2017).

The logic to internalize: a normal serum B12 with normal MMA and normal homocysteine is genuinely reassuring. A "normal" serum B12 with elevated MMA is a red flag the standard test alone would have hidden. This is why symptoms change everything — neurological complaints justify looking past a comfortable serum number to the functional layer beneath it.

Closing the loop: B12, folate, and macrocytic anemia

Back in the CBC chapter you met macrocytic anemia — anemia with abnormally large red blood cells, flagged by a high MCV — and we promised an explanation. Here it is.

Making a red blood cell requires copying DNA rapidly. Both B12 and folate are essential for that DNA synthesis. When either is deficient, developing red cells can't finish dividing properly: they keep growing but can't split, so they emerge too large. That's the macrocytosis. Because the mechanism is shared, B12 deficiency and folate deficiency produce a nearly identical blood picture — which is why a high MCV points to both as suspects, and why you can't tell them apart from the CBC alone.

The trap in treating the wrong one

This shared pathway creates a genuinely dangerous pitfall. Folate can partly "rescue" the anemia of B12 deficiency — giving folate lets the red cells mature, so the MCV normalizes and the blood count looks better. But folate does nothing for the neurological damage B12 deficiency causes. So you can mask the visible warning sign (the anemia) while the nerve damage silently progresses. This is exactly why confirming which nutrient is deficient matters, and why B12 deficiency with neurological symptoms is firmly a matter for medical evaluation, not self-treatment (Stabler, 2013; Green et al., 2017).

Notice how the two halves of this chapter converge on one discipline. Vitamin D taught you to read a marker in the context of when and who; B12 taught you that a normal marker can hide a real problem; and macrocytic anemia ties B12 and folate together into a picture no single number resolves. In every case the move is the same: confirm before you conclude.

Think About It

A CBC shows a high MCV. Someone reads online that "folate fixes big red cells" and starts a high-dose folate supplement. Their next CBC looks normal. Why might this be exactly the wrong outcome — and what did they fail to confirm first?

When to route to a professional

A recurring principle of this course: your job is to read the signal wisely, not to diagnose. Some results are signs that warrant medical evaluation, full stop. For these two markers:

Vitamin D: frank deficiency (well below the sufficiency line), especially with bone pain, muscle weakness, or falls, warrants clinical attention rather than experimental self-dosing. Very high levels from over-supplementation also warrant review.

B12: any neurological symptoms — persistent tingling, numbness, balance trouble, cognitive change — warrant evaluation regardless of what the serum B12 says. A high MCV on a CBC warrants working out which deficiency is at play before treating. And because folate can mask B12-related anemia while nerve damage continues, self-treating a suspected deficiency is precisely the wrong instinct.

Reading your bloodwork well means knowing both what a number can tell you and where its authority ends.

Key Takeaways

  • The standard vitamin D test measures 25(OH)D, the storage form — and it swings seasonally, by roughly 10 ng/mL peak-to-trough, so always note the collection date before interpreting.
  • Watch units: 1 ng/mL ≈ 2.5 nmol/L. A "sufficient" summer value can still leave you deficient in late winter, so aim for year-round headroom.
  • The gap between "sufficient" (~20 ng/mL, bone-based) and "optimal" (~30–50 ng/mL for broader outcomes) is a genuine, unresolved scientific debate — hold any higher target with humility, not as dogma.
  • Supplementation moves vitamin D predictably — roughly 1 ng/mL per 100 IU daily — but the response shrinks at higher doses and higher body fat, so re-test rather than assume.
  • A "normal" serum B12 does not rule out deficiency: about 28% of B12-deficient neurological patients had normal blood counts. MMA and homocysteine confirm what B12 is doing inside cells.
  • B12 and folate share the DNA-synthesis pathway, so both cause macrocytic (large-cell) anemia — and folate can mask B12 anemia while nerve damage continues, making confirmation essential.
  • Neurological symptoms, frank deficiency, or an unexplained high MCV are signs that warrant medical evaluation — not a self-treatment project.
Looking Ahead

Next we turn from single nutrients to the metabolic panel — glucose, HbA1c, and the markers of how your body handles fuel over time. You'll see the same theme evolve once more: a fasting glucose is a snapshot, HbA1c is a moving average, and "in range" hides a spectrum of trajectories long before anything crosses a diagnostic line.
